title: The merchant who let it go
told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a good thing you did once that nobody ever noticed?
options: keep them in mind. today says they aren’t lost.
that’s okay. some of the best ones get forgotten. listen.

steps.line: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told of a merchant, long ago, who lent money to people. When a debt came due and someone couldn’t pay, he did something unusual.

steps.q: The merchant tells his helpers to let the debt go. What reason do you think he gives?
o: “Maybe God will let us go too.”
steps.why: He let it go, and hoped for the same. In the saying, his words are to overlook the one in hardship, so that God might overlook him.

steps.line: “Let it go,” he told his helpers. “Maybe God will let us go too.”
When his account was called, a saying tells, nothing good was found in it, except this one habit of letting debts go.
And God said, “I am more worthy of letting go than he is. Let him go.”

steps.q: In the saying, God answers, “I am more worthy of letting go than he is.” What does that line suggest?
o: God outdoes the mercy people show
He’d earned it, fair and square
Debts don’t count on that Day
steps.why: The merchant hoped for a little mercy and got God’s, which is bigger. Many scholars note the saying is about mercy to people in hardship.

steps.line: Every prayer, right after the two names of mercy, says: “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” Din means repayment, what each is due. Its root also gives dayn, debt.

steps.pre: Din means repayment, what each is due. It’s also the everyday Arabic word for
steps.why: Religion: a way of life you live and answer for. It’s the din in the Qur’an’s “there is no compulsion in religion.”

steps.line: And nothing quiet is lost. A saying teaches: a good deed you meant to do, even one you never got to, is written down as a whole good deed.
steps.label: today

steps.line: And a wrong you meant to do, then let go of for God’s sake, is written as a good deed too. The angry text, deleted before it was sent.
steps.label: today

steps.q: A good deed you only meant to do is written as one. What about a good deed you actually do?
o: Written once, same as the plan
Written as two: plan and deed
Written ten times over, or more
steps.why: The same saying: ten times, up to seven hundred, or many more. And a wrong actually done is written as only one.

say: here’s what i love. the merchant’s whole hope fit in one line: maybe God will let us go too. and he was right.
in islam, the day of judgment is real, and every account is settled. but the one who holds it was just named merciful, twice. the account is in kind hands.

steps.q: The prayer names God merciful twice, then “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” From the merchant’s story, why might that order matter?
o: The Judge is the one just called merciful
Mercy ends when the Day begins
steps.why: The reckoning is held by mercy. Many readers say that order is the whole point.

today.say: the qur’an says that letting a struggling person’s debt go, as charity, is better for you. so today, let one small debt go: a favor owed, a coffee never paid back, a small grudge. leave the account with God.
options: lovely. that’s the merchant’s whole secret.
good. small ones count. nothing quiet is lost.

sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2078 and 3480; Sahih Muslim 1562 (Abu Hurayrah: a merchant used to lend to people; when he saw someone in hardship he told his young helpers, “Overlook him, perhaps Allah will overlook us”; so Allah overlooked him)

Sahih Muslim 1561 (Abu Mas‘ud: a man was called to account and nothing good was found for him except that he dealt with people and told his helpers to let off the one in hardship; Allah said, “We are more worthy of that than he; let him off”)
Qur’an 1:4 (“Owner of the Day of Judgment,” Pickthall)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6491; Sahih Muslim 131 (a good deed intended but not done is written as a complete good deed; a bad deed intended and then left is written as a complete good deed)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7501 (the bad deed left “for My sake” is written as a good deed)
Qur’an 2:280 (if the debtor is in hardship, give time until ease; to remit it as charity is better for you)
Din and dayn (debt) from the root d-y-n: Lane, An Arabic-English Lexicon
check: Muslim 1561 has God speak with the royal “We” (“We are more worthy of that than he”); the caption uses “I” to avoid confusion. Confirm.
The story joins two reports (Bukhari 2078 for the merchant’s words, Muslim 1561 for the reckoning); they may be the same man. Confirm.
Din glossed as “repayment, what each one is due” (jaza’), with dayn, debt, from the same root d-y-n. Confirm the gloss.
Tomorrow’s title “You alone.” stands for day 15 (Qur’an 1:5), whose lesson isn’t written yet.
